en: Śrī Śuka said:
The last of the Bārhadrathas will be named Purañjaya;
his minister, Śunaka, having killed his master and [installed] his own son—
The son of King Pālaka, known as Pradyota, will be the founder [of the dynasty];
his son will be Viśākhayūpa, and from him will come Rājaka.
Nandivardhana will be his son; these are the five Pradyotas.
One hundred and thirty-eight kings will rule the earth;
after them, Śiśunāga shall arise, and his son will be Kākavarṇa.
Kṣemadharmā will be his son, and Kṣetrajña will be born of Kṣemadharmā.

Vidhisāra will be his son, and Jātaśatru will follow him. Darbhaka will be his son, and Ajaya is recorded as the son of Darbhaka. Nandivardhana will be the son of Ajaya, and Mahānandi will be the son after him.

O best of the Kurus, these ten Śiśunāga kings will rule the earth for three hundred and sixty years during the Kali age. O King, the powerful son of Mahānandi will be born from the womb of a Śūdra woman.

A certain Nanda, the lord of Mahāpadma, will be the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas; thereafter, kings will arise who are mostly Śūdras and unrighteous. He, with his command unchallenged, will rule the earth under a single umbrella.
Mahāpadma will rule like a second Bhārgava;
he shall have eight sons, headed by Sumālya,
who will enjoy this earth as kings for a hundred years.
A certain brāhmaṇa will deliver the nine Nandas who have sought his protection;
in their absence, the Mauryas will indeed rule the earth in the Kali age.
That same brāhmaṇa will indeed consecrate Candragupta upon the throne.
His son will be Vārisāra, and from him will come Aśokavardhana.
Suyaśas will be his [successor], and Saṅgata will be the son of Suyaśas. From him will come Śāliśūka, and after him Somaśarmā will arise.

Then Śatadhanvan will be his [son], and from him will come Bṛhadratha. O scion of the Kuru lineage, these ten Maurya kings shall rule the earth for one hundred and thirty-seven years during the Kali age.
From him, Agnimitra will arise; from him, Sujyeṣṭha will be born. Then Vasumitra and Bhadraka will follow, and Pulinda will be his son.
After that, Ghoṣa will be the son, and from him Vajramitra will come to be.
O best of the Kurus, from that Bhāgavata will come Devabhūti;
these ten Śuṅgas shall enjoy the earth for more than a hundred years.
Thereafter, O King, this earth will pass to the Kāṇvas, who possess few virtues.
Having killed the lustful Śuṅga Devabhūti, the high-minded minister Vasudeva of the Kāṇva lineage will himself rule the kingdom. His son will be Bhūmitra, and his son will be Nārāyaṇa.
These Kāṇvāyanas shall enjoy the earth for three hundred and forty-five years during the Kali age;
and having killed the Kāṇva Suśarman, his powerful Śūdra servant [will rule].
A most wicked man of the Andhra race will rule over the earth for some time;
then his brother, named Kṛṣṇa, will become the lord of the earth. His son will be Śrī-Śāntakarṇa, and Paurṇamāsa will be his son.
Lambodara was his son; from him came King Cibilaka.
From Cibilaka came Meghasvāti, and from him came Aṭamāna.
Aniṣṭakarman was his [Aṭamāna's] son, as was Hāleya; Talaka was his [Hāleya's] offspring.
His son will be Purīṣabhīru, and from him the king Sunandana; then Cakora, Bahava, and Śivasvāti, the subduer of enemies;
his son will be Gomatī, and from him Purīmān shall arise.
Medaśiras, Śivaskanda, and his son Yajñaśrī; then Vijaya, his son, whose son will be Bhāvya; then Candravijña and Salomadhi—these thirty kings [will rule] for four hundred years.
O descendant of Kuru, fifty-six kings will enjoy the earth;
seven Āvabhṛtyas, ten Gardabhin kings,
and sixteen Kaṅka rulers will follow, all of them exceedingly greedy.
After that, eight Yavanas will arise, followed by fourteen Turuṣkas;
then ten Guruṇḍas and eleven Maulas. These shall rule the earth for one thousand years.
They, the eleven original [kings], shall enjoy the earth for ninety-nine hundred years,
my dear; when they have passed away, there will then be kings in Kilakilā, namely Bhūtananda and Vaṅgiri.
Śiśunandi, his brother Yaśonandi, and Pravīraka—
these shall indeed rule for one hundred and six years.
They will have thirteen sons who will be the Bāhlikas.
Then there will be the kṣatriya Puṣpamitra, and likewise Durmitra;
these seven kings will rule for one period of time. There will be seven Andhras, seven Kauśalas, the lords of Vidūra, and from them indeed the Niṣadhas.
Among the Magadhas, there will be Purañjaya, known as Viśvasphūrji;
he will transform the castes into Pulindas, Yadus, and Madrakas, and that evil-minded one will establish subjects who are largely devoid of the Vedic path.
That heroic one, having exterminated the Kṣatriyas, will enjoy the earth protected by him from Padmavatī city along the Ganges as far as Prayāga; likewise,
the Saurāṣṭras, Āvantyas, Ābhīras, Śūras, Arbudas, and Mālavas [will be under his sway].

The twice-born will become *vrātyas*, and the rulers of men will be mostly *śūdras*. *Śūdras*, *vrātyas*, and other barbarians (*mlecchas*) devoid of Vedic luster will enjoy the banks of the Indus, the Candrabhāgā, the Kauntī, and the region of Kashmir.
O King, these rulers will be equal in their duration of time and will consist mostly of barbarians;
they will be devoted to unrighteousness and falsehood, insignificant and servile, and possessed of fierce anger.
They will be slayers of women, children, cows, and the twice-born, and they will show no regard for the wives or wealth of others.
With the sun mostly risen and set [in their conduct], possessing little strength and short lifespans,
unrefined and devoid of sacred rites, shrouded by passion and ignorance— those Mlecchas in the form of Kṣatriyas will devour your subjects.
Those provinces will have him as their lord; following his character, conduct, and speech, they—tormented by one another and by kings—will go to their destruction.
Śrī Śuka said:
Therefore, O King, in the course of time, which is all-powerful, righteousness, truth, purity, forgiveness, and compassion will perish; likewise, lifespan, strength, memory,
and even wealth shall decline among men in the Kali age, as shall the excellence of their birth, conduct, and virtues.
In the establishment of dharma and justice, force alone is indeed the cause;
in marriage, mutual desire is the motive; in worldly affairs, it is mere illusion (māyā);
and in femininity, masculinity, and even the status of a Brahmin, it is simply attachment and the sacred thread.
The mere external mark is the cause for the mutual confusion of the stages of life (āśramas). Lack of livelihood leads to weakness in moral conduct; in scholarship, it leads to verbal frivolity.
Poverty alone is the cause of wickedness, whereas hypocrisy is the cause of apparent goodness.

In marriage, the very act of acceptance is the bath; adornment is merely the washing away of impurities. A sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) is simply a distant water source; beauty is the maintenance of one's hair. One's own purpose is merely filling one's belly; indeed, in truthfulness, there is only boldness.
Dexterity in maintaining a family, the pursuit of dharma for the sake of fame—
thus, when the circle of the earth is crowded with such wicked subjects,
whichever king among the Brahmins, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, or Śūdras becomes powerful shall [rule].
For the subjects, their wives and wealth having been seized by greedy, merciless Kṣatriyas who follow the ways of bandits, will flee to the mountains and forests,
subsisting on vegetables, roots, meat, honey, fruits, flowers, and grains.
Due to drought, the people will perish, oppressed by famine and taxes;
tormented by cold, wind, heat, the rainy season, and frost, they will suffer from one another,
as well as from hunger, thirst, diseases, and anxiety.
In the Kali age, the maximum lifespan of human beings is thirty or twenty years,
as the bodies of embodied beings waste away due to the defects of the Kali.

When the social orders consist mostly of *śūdras*, when cows consist mostly of goats, when hermitages consist mostly of houses, when kinsmen consist mostly of relations by marriage,
when medicinal herbs consist mostly of tiny seeds, and when stationary plants consist mostly of *śamī* trees;
When the clouds are filled with lightning, when houses have become almost deserted,

and when people in the Kali age have become as harsh-natured as donkeys— when the age has thus nearly reached its end— the Blessed Lord will descend with his essence for the protection of righteousness.
The birth of Viṣṇu, the teacher of all moving and non-moving beings, the Lord, the Self of all— for the protection of the dharma of the virtuous and for the removal of their karma—
was from a high-souled Brāhmaṇa who was the chief of the village of Śambhala.
In the house of Viṣṇuyaśas, Kalki will appear;
mounted upon his swift horse Devadatta, the Lord of the World,
endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers, will subdue the wicked with his sword.
Wandering upon the earth on a swift horse, he of incomparable splendor,
disguised in the attire of a king, will slay the bandits by the millions.
Then, indeed, their minds shall become truly pure.
When all the bandits have been slain, the people of the cities and the countryside— who have touched the wind carrying the exceedingly holy fragrance from the body-unguents of Vāsudeva—
will indeed experience a most abundant increase in progeny.

When the Blessed Lord Kalki, Hari the Lord of Dharma, has descended while Vāsudeva— the embodiment of pure goodness— resides within the heart, then the Kṛta age will prevail and the procreation of beings will be characterized by goodness (*sattva*).
When the moon, the sun, as well as Tiṣya and Bṛhaspati,
shall come together in a single zodiacal sign, then the Kṛta age will begin;
and those kings who have passed away, those who are present, and those who are yet to come— [all these shall arise].
These descendants of the Moon and the Sun have been described by way of summary,
beginning from your own birth up until the consecration of Nanda.
This period consists of one thousand one hundred and fifteen years.
Of the seven ṛṣis, those two who are first seen risen in the sky—
between them, whichever constellation is seen at night level with them,
by that [constellation] the ṛṣis remain conjoined for a hundred years of men.

O twice-born ones, at this time the moon has entered the constellation Maghā, which belongs to you; and that sun of the Lord Viṣṇu, known as Kṛṣṇa, has departed for heaven. Now Kali has entered the world, since people now delight in sin.
As long as the Lord of Ramā remained touching the earth with his two lotus feet,
Kali was indeed unable to invade the world.
For it is when the seven celestial sages move through the constellation Maghā that Kali gains power.
Then the Kali age, consisting of twelve hundred years,
will indeed set in; when the great sages depart from Maghā to go toward Pūrvāṣāḍhā,
then, starting from the time of Nanda, this Kali age will begin to increase.
On that very day when Kṛṣṇa ascended to heaven,
those who know the past declare that the Kali-yuga had commenced.
At the end of the fourth millennium of divine years, however, the Kṛta-yuga begins once again.
Then the minds of men will become self-illuminating.
Thus, just as this lineage of Manu is enumerated on earth,
so too should the various lineages of Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and Brahmins be known in each successive age.
Of these high-souled persons, whose names and characteristics remain as mere topics of discourse, only their fame persists on earth.
Devāpi was the brother of Śāntanu, and Maru was born of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
In the village of Kalāpa, those two, endowed with the power of great yoga, will reside;
having come here at the end of the Kali age, instructed by Vāsudeva, they will propagate the dharma consisting of the [four] social classes and [four] stages of life, just as it was before.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali—these constitute the four yugas.
By this sequential process, O King, they proceed among living beings on earth. Thus have these kings, as well as others, been described by me.

Having developed a sense of ownership toward the earth, they eventually abandon it and meet their end; O King, even one who bears the title of "king" becomes known at last as nothing more than worms, excrement, or ashes.
What self-interest does such a person, who harms living beings for his own sake, truly understand, since he is destined for hell?
"How was this entire earth maintained by my ancestors, and how will it be maintained for my son, my grandson, or for those born in my lineage?
For the ignorant, having assumed a body composed of fire, water, and food, identify with it as their very self."

Having abandoned both the earth and the sense of "mine-ness," they have at last vanished from sight. O King, all those lords of the earth who enjoyed the land by their might have been reduced by time to mere stories, and even those stories are now but words.
Śrī Śuka said:
Seeing the kings intent on victory over him, this earth laughed: "Alas! These kings, who are but playthings of Death, desire to conquer me."
This desire of kings, even for those who are wise, is in vain,
since those monarchs place excessive trust in this body which is like foam.
Having first conquered the six internal enemies, we shall then conquer the royal ministers.
"Therefore, we shall conquer his thorns— the ministers, citizens, and chief elephants— in this sequence, and thus take the earth girt by the oceans.
With their hearts bound by such hope, they do not see Death standing near them.

"Having conquered the ocean-bound earth, they enter the sea by their might. O best of the Kurus, how insignificant is this compared to self-conquest; the fruit of self-conquest is liberation, which even the Manus and their sons abandoned."

They have departed from the battle just as they came; those of little intelligence will conquer me. Indeed, for the sake of my interests, conflict arises among fathers, sons, and brothers when the minds of the wicked are bound by attachment to a kingdom.
"To me alone belongs this entire earth; it is not yours, you fool!"—speaking thus, kings who contend with one another kill each other and die for my sake.
Such were Pṛthu, Purūravas, Gādhi, Nahuṣa, Bharata, and Arjuna.
Māndhātṛ, Sagara, Rāma, Khaṭvāṅga, Dhundhumāra, Raghu,
Tṛṇabindu, Yayāti, Śaryāti, Śantanu, Gaya,
Bhagīratha, Kuvalayāśva, Kakutstha, Naiṣadha, and Nṛga.
Hiraṇyakaśipu, Vṛtra, Rāvaṇa— the one who made the world cry out— Namuci, Śambara, Bhauma, Hiraṇyākṣa, and Tāraka;
as well as many other Daityas who were powerful kings.
All were knowers of all things, heroes, and all were unconquered conquerors; yet,
O Lord, though they possessed the nature of mortals, they maintained a sense of "mineness" toward me,
and in time they were reduced to mere stories, their purposes unfulfilled.

O Lord, these stories of yours concerning those most exalted who have departed to the other world have been narrated for the sake of spreading their fame throughout the worlds, with the desire to impart spiritual knowledge and detachment; they are the manifestations of the power of Your speech, yet not the ultimate truth itself.
However, that which is the constant chanting of the virtues of the One of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka) is the destroyer of all inauspiciousness.
One who desires pure devotion for Kṛṣṇa should constantly and repeatedly listen to that very [account].
The King said:
O Blessed One, by what means do people in the Kali age overcome the defects of the Kali?
O sage, tell me how they will destroy those accumulated [sins], as well as the ages (yugas), the characteristics of the ages, the measurement of the dissolution and the kalpa,
and the movement of Time, which is the form of the Lord, the high-souled Viṣṇu.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, in the Kṛta age, dharma exists with four quarters, upheld by the people born in that age;
its four quarters, O monarch, are truth, compassion, austerity, and charity, belonging to the Lord.
Contented, compassionate, friendly, peaceful, self-controlled, and patient—
such people were for the most part mendicants who delighted in the Self and possessed equal vision.
In the Tretā age, one quarter of the limbs of Dharma gradually diminished.

O King, at that time, the four quarters of unrighteousness—falsehood, violence, discontent, and strife—will prevail; yet those devoted to ritual action and austerity will not be excessively cruel or licentious. The social orders (varṇas), headed by the Brahmins, will be devoted to the three goals of life and will be advanced in the knowledge of the three Vedas.
In the Dvāpara age, austerity, truthfulness, compassion, and charity lose half their power;
for dharma is characterized by unrighteousness through violence, discontent, falsehood, and hatred.
[Yet there remain] those of great renown and noble character, devoted to the study and recitation of the Vedas.

The householders were prosperous and joyful, as were the social orders, with the Kṣatriyas and twice-born leading them. But in the Kali age, a quarter of the pillars of dharma will be diminished by the increasing causes of unrighteousness; indeed, even that quarter will perish at the end.
In that [age], the subjects will be greedy, ill-behaved, merciless, harboring dry enmity, unfortunate, and possessed of excessive thirst; they will be mostly Śūdras and slaves.
The qualities of goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas) are seen in a person.
Impelled by time, these indeed revolve within the self;
when the mind, intellect, and senses manifest in the mode of goodness (sattva),
one should know that to be the Kṛta-yuga, for there is a delight in knowledge and austerity.

O intelligent one, know that when embodied beings possess devotion toward ritual acts performed for desired rewards and toward fame, that is the Tretā age, characterized by the mode of passion (rajas). Furthermore,
when greed, discontent, pride, hypocrisy, and envy prevail—
The Dvāpara age is characterized by ritual actions performed for selfish desires, as well as by passion (rajas) and ignorance (tamas).
When illusion, falsehood, sloth, sleep, violence,
despondency, grief, delusion, fear, and wretchedness prevail, that is known as the Kali age, which is dominated by ignorance (tāmasa).
Therefore, mortals will be small-minded, of meager fortune, and gluttonous; men will be lustful and destitute of wealth, while women will be wanton and unchaste.
The provinces will be overrun by bandits, and the Vedas will be defiled by heretics.
Kings will devour their subjects; twice-born men will be devoted only to their genitals and bellies; students will be devoid of vows and impure; mendicants will become householders;
ascetics will dwell in villages; and renunciates will be excessively greedy.
With short statures, great appetites, many offspring, and devoid of shame,
they will constantly speak harshly; being petty merchants and cheats, they will practice theft, sorcery, and great acts of violence.
Even in times of no distress, they will consider even honest livelihood to be contemptible;

servants will abandon their master, though he be the most excellent of all, if he is destitute of wealth; and husbands will abandon a servant who has fallen into misfortune, as well as cows that yield no milk, even if they are of noble lineage.

In the Kali age, men will abandon their fathers, brothers, friends, and kinsmen; they will be devoted only to sexual pleasure and friendship, will converse with their sisters-in-law and brothers-in-law, and being wretched and dominated by women, they will become Śūdras who subsist on the outward appearance of asceticism while living off the gifts of others.
Ignorant of righteousness, they will ascend to high seats and preach dharma;
with minds constantly anxious, O King, they will be emaciated by famine and distressed by the fear of drought upon a land devoid of food.
In the Kali age, people will be bereft of clothing, food, drink, bedding, sexual pleasure, bathing, and ornaments; appearing like Piśācas,
they will abandon their friendships and quarrel over even a single cowrie shell.
These base men, who nourish only their genitals and bellies, will abandon their dear lives and even kill their own kin; they will not protect even their aged parents,
nor their sons, nor their wives born of noble families.

O King, in the Kali age, mortals— whose minds are generally distracted by heretical doctrines— will for the most part fail to worship the Lord Acyuta, the supreme teacher of the worlds, whose lotus feet are bowed to by the lords of the three realms. Yet,
even a man who is helpless, whether dying, suffering, falling, or stumbling, if he utters His name...
With the bolt of karma cast off, he attains the supreme goal; yet in the Kali age, people will not worship him.
However, the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Person, dwelling within the heart, removes all the defects of men caused by the Kali age, whether arising from material objects, place, or the self.
Whether heard, glorified, meditated upon, worshiped, or even merely respected,
the Blessed One, dwelling within the hearts of men, shakes off the impurities of tens of thousands of births—
just as fire residing within gold destroys the base alloy.

In this way, Viṣṇu, who has entered the self of yogis, does not grant the inner self absolute purity through knowledge, austerity, breath-control, friendliness, bathing at sacred fords, vows, charity, or recitation,
as He does when the infinite Blessed One resides within the heart.

Therefore, O King, with all your soul, place Keśava within your heart; for one who dies with focused attention upon Him goes to the supreme goal. The Blessed Lord, the Supreme Controller, is to be meditated upon by those who are dying.
O dear one, the Self of all, who is the refuge of all, leads [the devotee] to His own state of being.
O King, although the Kali age is a reservoir of faults, it possesses one great virtue:
by the mere chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s names, one becomes free from attachment and attains the Supreme.
That which is attained by meditating on Viṣṇu in the Kṛta age, by worshipping Him with sacrifices in the Tretā age,
or by performing service in the Dvāpara age, is attained in the Kali age simply through the chanting of Hari’s names.
Śrī Śuka said:

O King, time has been described as beginning with the *paramāṇu* and ending with two *parārdhas*; you have also heard the measurement of the *yugas*. Now hear also of the *kalpa* and the dissolution (*laya*).
A thousand cycles of the four *yugas* is said to be one day of Brahmā.

O lord of the people, that period during which the fourteen Manus exist is called a *kalpa*. At the end of that, there is a dissolution (*pralaya*) of equal duration; this is declared to be one night of Brahmā. Indeed, within that time, these three worlds are prepared for dissolution.

This is declared to be the occasional dissolution (naimittika-pralaya), wherein the Creator of the universe, having brought the entire world into himself, the self-born one, reclines upon his infinite seat. This occurs when two *parārdhas* of the life of Brahmā, the supreme lord, have passed away.
Then the seven constituent principles (prakṛtis) indeed dissolve for the sake of dissolution;
this, O King, is the elemental dissolution (prākṛtika-pralaya),
wherein the cosmic egg— the aggregate— is destroyed when [the causal waters] have arrived.

O King, Parjanya shall not rain upon the earth for a hundred years. Then, when food is utterly absent, the people— afflicted by hunger and oppressed by time— will gradually go to their destruction, devouring one another.

The sun of the dissolution (Sāṃvartaka), with its terrible rays, drinks up all moisture— whether from the oceans, the bodies of beings, or the earth— and releases none at all. Thereafter, the fire of destruction (Saṃvartaka) arises from the mouth of Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Then, fanned by the force of the wind, it burns the hollows of the earth;
with its flames from above, below, and all around,
the cosmic egg— being consumed like a ball of dried cow-dung— shines forth.
Then, for more than a hundred years, a fierce wind known as the *sāṃvartaka* blows,
making the sky grey and shrouded in dust;
thereafter, O dear one, numerous clouds of various colors appear.
For a hundred years they rain down and roar with violent sounds;
thereafter, the entire universe, within the cavity of the cosmic egg, becomes a single expanse of water.
Then, during the dissolution by water, the waters swallow the quality of smell belonging to the earth;
once its smell has been swallowed, the earth is fit for dissolution.
Then the fire swallows the taste of the waters, and those waters, now devoid of taste, dissolve into it.

Then the wind devours the form of fire; when that [form] is removed, fire merges into the wind. O King, the ether then devours the quality of the wind, and the wind indeed enters the ether; thereafter, it [the wind] also enters the quality of the ether.

The source of the elements (bhūtādi) swallows sound, and space dissolves into it; the fiery principle (taijasa) swallows the senses, O dear one, and the transformative principle (vaikārika) swallows the gods along with the modes (guṇas). The Great Principle (mahat) swallows the ego (ahaṅkāra), and the modes—sattva and the others—swallow that [Great Principle].
O King, impelled by time, the unmanifest (avyākṛta) devours the qualities (guṇas).
Its qualities, such as transformation and the like, do not arise from the divisions of time;
it is beginningless, endless, unmanifest, eternal, and the imperishable cause.
Therein, neither speech, nor mind, nor the qualities of goodness, passion, and ignorance exist; nor do these principles beginning with the Great One (mahat);
nor are there the vital breaths, the senses, or their presiding deities, nor indeed any structural arrangement corresponding to the worlds.
It is neither the dreaming state, nor the waking state, nor the state of deep sleep; it is not ether, water, earth, air, fire, or the sun.

They declare that fundamental state to be like deep sleep, like a void, and beyond the reach of logic; for this is the natural dissolution (*prākṛtika-laya*) of both the Person (*puruṣa*) and the Unmanifest (*avyakta*),
when their powers, driven by Time, become helpless and utterly merge away.
Knowledge, which has the intellect and the objects of the senses as its form, appears with that [knowledge] as its locus;
yet that which is subject to appearance and disappearance, being neither distinct from nor separate from the object of sight, is a non-entity, like a beginning and an end.
Just as a lamp, the eye, and form are not separate from light, so too are they not separate from consciousness.
In this way, the intellect, the senses, and the subtle elements cannot exist apart from one of the three states of reality.
Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are said to be functions of the intellect;
O King, this diversity within the inner self is merely an illusion.
Just as clouds appear and disappear in the sky,
so does this universe— composed of parts— arise and dissolve within Brahman; for here, Brahman is declared to be the reality that constitutes all composite things.
Without a substrate (artha), they could not be perceived, just as threads cannot be perceived apart from a cloth.
That which is apprehended through both the universal and the particular is an illusion;
because they are mutually dependent, everything that has a beginning and an end is unreal.

Even when a transformation is being perceived, it cannot be defined as even an atom’s worth of something apart from the inner self (pratyag-ātman), provided it were equal to consciousness like the Self itself.
For one who lacks true knowledge might imagine a plurality in that which is real, yet no such plurality exists.
Just as there is a distinction between two openings, or between two lights, or like two winds;
just as gold is fashioned in many ways by men through various activities on the paths of worldly commerce;
even so is the Lord Adhokṣaja described by people through worldly and Vedic words.
Just as a cloud produced by the sun and seen by the sun obscures the darkness of the eye— which is itself a portion of the sun—
so too am I, possessing the qualities of Brahman, perceived by Him.
When the dense cloud that binds the Self— which is a portion of Brahman—
is dispersed by the light of the sun, one perceives the sun in its true nature; likewise,
when the ego, which is the limiting adjunct of the Self, perishes through inquiry, then one should remember [the Supreme].

O scorcher of foes, when one has thus severed the bondage of the self consisting of the egoity born of māyā by means of this weapon of discrimination, and remains established in the experience of the Self as Acyuta— that, my dear, they call the ultimate dissolution (samplava) for all beings, beginning with Brahmā, occurring at all times.
Some who possess subtle knowledge declare that creation and dissolution are merely the various states of things subject to transformation,
which are constantly and swiftly carried away by the force of the stream of time;
these states are the causes of birth and dissolution.
By this time, which is without beginning or end and is the very form of the Lord,
the various states of dissolution are not perceived, just as the positions of the luminaries in the sky cannot be seen; these are the eternal, occasional, and elemental dissolutions.
And thus has been described the ultimate course of time; such is its nature.

O best of the Kurus, these stories of the pastimes of Nārāyaṇa, the architect of the universe and the abode of all existence, have been told to you in brief; even the Unborn Lord is not able to describe them in their entirety.
For one who desires to cross the ocean of worldly existence, which is exceedingly difficult to traverse,
there is no other raft than the cultivation of the essence of the stories of the divine pastimes of the Supreme Person, the Blessed Lord.
To a person afflicted by the forest fire of manifold sufferings,
the imperishable sage Nārāyaṇa formerly spoke this Purāṇa-saṃhitā to Nārada, and he [Nārada] spoke it to Kṛṣṇa-Dvaipāyana.
O great king, that blessed Bādarāyaṇa will indeed,
being pleased, relate this *Bhāgavata Saṃhitā*, which is equal to the Vedas;
and he, Sūta, will recite it to the sages at Naimiṣa.
O best of the Kurus, having been questioned by Śaunaka and others during the long sacrificial session (dīrghasatra),
the venerable Śuka said:
"In this regard, the Lord Hari, the soul of the universe, is now described in detail."

From whose grace Brahmā was born and from whose anger Rudra arose—O King, abandon this animal-like notion that "you will die. You were not born before, nor did you exist as a body today; you shall not perish.
Having existed in the form of sons, grandsons, and so forth, you shall no longer exist;
for like fire is distinct from its fuel, the body and such, you are separate from them—
just as one experiences in a dream the decapitation of one's own head or one's own death.
Because one perceives [the Self] as distinct from the body, the Self is indeed unborn and immortal.
Just as when a jar is broken, the space within the jar becomes the universal space as it was before,
so too, when the body dies, the living being attains Brahman once again.
The mind indeed creates for itself bodies, qualities, and actions;
that mind is created by Māyā, and from that arises the transmigratory existence of the individual soul (jīva).
As long as the conjunction of oil, the wick, and fire persists, [so does the cycle continue].

Just as long as there is the nature of a lamp, so too does the existence produced by the body arise and perish through the fluctuations of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas*. In that regard, the Self is self-luminous, being beyond both the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*).
Like space, he is the support, fixed and comparable to the infinite; therefore,
O Lord, perceive the Self as abiding within yourself by means of the intellect imbued with inference and through constant meditation upon Vāsudeva.
"Urged by the words of the brāhmaṇas, Takṣaka shall not burn you;
nor will the messengers of death consume you, for you are the Lord, the death of deaths.
I am Brahman, the supreme abode; I am Brahman, the highest state."
Having thus reflected and having established yourself within the partless Self,
you will no longer perceive the body or the universe as separate from the Self, even while seeing Takṣaka biting your foot and licking it with his venomous mouths.
"O dear one, O King, I have related to you that which your soul asked regarding the activities of Hari, the Soul of the Universe. What more do you wish to hear?
Sūta said:
Having heard this spoken by the sage Vyāsa’s son, who is impartial and perceives the Self in all beings, Parīkṣit approached the soles of his feet with his head bowed.
With palms joined in reverence, that son of Viṣṇu spoke this to him.
The King said:
"I am perfected; I have been graced by you, whose nature is compassion."
That Hari, who is without beginning or end, was personally heard by me;
yet I do not consider this to be very wonderful, for it is the natural disposition of the great whose souls are fixed in Acyuta to show favor toward ignorant beings tormented by suffering.
We have heard this Purāṇic compendium from you,
in which the Blessed Lord of excellent renown is indeed described.
O Blessed One, I do not fear death from Takṣaka or others.
You have shown me the fearless state of Brahman-nirvāṇa, which I have now entered. O Brahman, grant me leave; I shall restrain my speech toward Adhokṣaja.
Having caused my mind, from which all desire has been released, to enter Him, I shall cast off my vital breaths.
"Through my steadfastness in knowledge and realized wisdom, ignorance has been dispelled by me;
you have shown me the supreme state of security, the abode of the Blessed Lord.
Sūta said:

Having been addressed thus, the Blessed Bādarāyaṇi took leave of him and departed together with the mendicants, honored by the god among men (Parīkṣit). Parīkṣit, the royal sage, [then beheld] the Self within himself by means of his own self.
Having composed himself, he meditated on the Supreme, motionless like a tree; seated upon sacrificial grass on the eastern bank of the Gaṅgā, facing north,
that great yogi had become Brahman, free from attachment, and his doubts were severed.
O brahmins, Takṣaka, dispatched by the enraged son of the twice-born and desiring to kill the king, saw Kaśyapa on the road as he was traveling;
having gratified that remover of poison with wealth, he turned him back.

Assuming the disguised form of a twice-born, he who could take any shape at will bit the king; while all embodied beings looked on, the body of the royal sage— who had already become one with Brahman— was instantly reduced to ashes by the fire of the serpent's venom.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose everywhere on the earth, in the sky, and in all directions;
indeed, all the gods, asuras, humans, and others were struck with wonder.
The celestial drums resounded, and the gandharvas and apsaras sang.
The gods, proclaiming "Well done!", rained down showers of flowers.
Having heard that his father had been devoured by Takṣaka, Janamejaya,
filled with rage, summoned the serpents at his sacrifice along with the twice-born brahmins.
Seeing the great serpents being consumed in the kindled fire at the snake-sacrifice, Takṣaka, agitated by fear, went to Indra for refuge. There,
King Parīkṣit did not see Takṣaka, but [instead saw] the twice-born brahmins.
Takṣaka said: "O Indra among kings, why does that lowest of serpents not burn? Śakra protects him because he has come to him for refuge;
paralyzed by him, that serpent therefore does not fall into the fire."
O descendant of Parikṣit, having heard this, the noble-minded officiating priests, together with Indra, asked:
"Why is Takṣaka not cast into the fire, O brāhmaṇas?
Having heard that, the brāhmaṇas offered Takṣaka along with Indra into the sacrificial fire.
"O Takṣaka, fall down here immediately along with Indra and the Maruts!"—
by these insults uttered by Brahmā, Indra was shaken from his place; he became bewildered in mind, together with his celestial chariot and Takṣaka.
Seeing Takṣaka falling from the sky along with his celestial chariot,
Bṛhaspati, the son of Aṅgiras, said to the king:
"O Indra among men, this king of serpents does not deserve to be killed by you."
By this [knowledge] one has drunk the nectar of immortality, or else one becomes free from old age and death.
O King, the life, death, and destiny of a living being are determined by its own karma alone;
there is no other giver of its pleasure and pain.
O King, when a living being meets its end through snakes, thieves, fire, lightning, hunger, thirst, disease, and so forth, it experiences the results of that commenced karma.
Therefore, O King, this sacrificial session (satra) of yours must be brought to completion; it is a rite of exorcism.
"Innocent snakes were burned by people; indeed, one must experience what is ordained.
Sūta said:
Having been addressed thus, he replied, "So be it," honoring the words of the great seer.
Having desisted from the snake-sacrifice, he worshipped the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati).

This very thing is the great illusion (māyā) of Viṣṇu, characterized by delusion, by which even those who have become his own self are bewildered among living beings through the functions of the material qualities (guṇas).

Where there is no hypocrite, it is resplendent with fearlessness; where, through the repeated discourse on the Self by those who speak of the Self, there is no talk of *māyā*; where there is no dispute based on various [theories], nor a mind characterized by the functions of resolve and doubt; where there is nothing to be created, being beyond both the creator and the creation, and where the individual soul (*jīva*)—endowed with the three qualities—is the Supreme Good, that is "I."

Having thus refuted these waves of the relationship between the oppressor and the oppressed, the sage should cease [all mental activity] and rest in that supreme state of Viṣṇu, which those desiring to cast off what is not that describe as "not this, not this" (neti neti),
embracing with their hearts that which is established within, having abandoned wickedness and being devoted to nothing else, with minds composed.
They attain this supreme abode of Viṣṇu,
in whom there is no wickedness arising from the body or home, such as the notions of "I" and "mine.
One should endure insults and should not despise anyone.
One should not harbor enmity toward anyone while inhabiting this body. Salutations to that Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa of unimpeded intellect,
by meditating upon whose lotus feet I have mastered this compendium.
Śrī Śaunaka said:
O gentle one, please tell us how the Vedas were divided and expounded by the high-souled disciples of Vyāsa, such as Paila and others,
who were masters of the Vedas.
Sūta said:
O Brahmin, from the heart of the self-composed Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, the Nāda arose from the ether; it is perceived through the restraint of the mental fluctuations.

O Brahman, by meditating upon which the yogis shake off the impurity of the self— consisting of substance, action, and agency— and attain the state from which there is no return; from that [impurity] arose the threefold *oṃkāra*, which has the unmanifest as its source and is the self-ruling Lord.
That which is the mark (*liṅga*) of the Blessed Brahman, the Supreme Self—
he who hears this *sphoṭa* with his ears closed and his vision fixed on the void;
that by which speech is manifested, whose manifestation is in space (*ākāśa*), and which belongs to the Self.
The Brāhmaṇa is the direct designator of the Supreme Self from His own abode;
he is the eternal seed of the Vedas, containing all mantras and Upaniṣads, O descendant of Bhṛgu. Indeed, his three constituent letters are those beginning with 'A'.
By means of which the three states— consisting of qualities (*guṇa*), names (*nāman*), and referents (*artha*)— are sustained;
from that [state], the unborn Lord created the traditional collection of syllables (*akṣara-samāmnāya*),
characterized by semivowels (*antastha*), sibilants (*ūṣman*), vowels (*svara*), stops (*sparśa*), short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and so forth.
With that [speech], the omnipresent Lord, desiring to expound the fourfold sacrificial ritual (*cāturhotra*),
taught his four sons— the *brahmarṣis* who were experts in the Veda— the four Vedas, together with the *vyāhṛtis* and the syllable *oṃ*.
Those teachers of dharma, in turn, instructed their own sons;
these [teachings] were received through a lineage by various disciples who maintained their vows,
and were then distributed by the great seers at the beginning of the Dvāpara age and subsequent yugas.

O Brahmana, observing that at the end of time people would have their lifespans diminished, their strength depleted, and their intellects clouded, the great sages, impelled by the Lord residing within their hearts, divided the Vedas. Furthermore, during this very interval, the Blessed One, the creator of the worlds, [appeared].
Requested by Brahmā, Śiva, and the other guardians of the worlds for the protection of dharma,
the omnipresent Lord, O fortunate one, descended through a portion of a portion of his own power into Satyavatī via Parāśara,
and divided the Veda into four parts.
Having extracted the collections of the Ṛg, Atharva, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas section by section,
he composed four *saṃhitās* with the mantras, like clusters of jewels.
Then that highly intelligent one, having summoned four disciples of those [Vedas], [entrusted them to them].
O Brahmin, the Lord gave one *saṃhitā* to each;
he spoke the first *saṃhitā*, known as the *Bahvṛca*, to Paila,
and the collection of *Yajus* mantras called *Nigada* to the one named Vaiśampāyana.
He taught the Sāman hymns and the Chāndogya Saṃhitā to Jaimini; likewise, he taught the collection known as the Atharvāṅgirasa to his own disciple Sumantu.
The sage Paila then recited his own Saṃhitā to Indrapramiti.
He [Bāṣkala] also spoke his own *saṃhitā* to his disciples;
having divided it into four parts, he taught it to Bodhya, Yājñavalkya, Bhārgava,
Parāśara, Agnimitra, and the self-possessed Indrapramiti.
He taught his own *saṃhitā* to the wise seer Māṇḍūkeya;
his disciple Devamitra taught it to Saubhari and others. Śākalya, his son, divided his own *saṃhitā* into five parts.

Jātūkarṇya, the disciple of that [Vaiśampāyana], imparted his own Saṃhitā along with the Nirukta to Vātsya, Mudgala, Śālīya, Gokhalya, and Śiśira; the sage then gave it to Balāka, Paila, Jābāla, and Viraja.

Bāṣkali compiled the Saṃhitā known as the Vālakhilya from the various Śākhās; Bhajya, Vālāyani, and Kāśāra likewise upheld it. Indeed, these Saṃhitās of the Bahvṛcas were maintained by these Brahmanical sages.

Having heard this expansion of the Vedas (*chandas*), one is liberated from all sins. Indeed, the disciples of Vaiśampāyana became the Caraka-Adhvaryus; they performed the vow of their own teacher as a means to expiate the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*).
And his disciple Yājñavalkya said: "O Blessed One, how much [remains] for me? I shall perform that most difficult practice which is of little substance for those who act.
Being thus addressed, the guru, becoming angry, said: "Go away! Enough of you!"
"O Brahmin, abandon at once what was studied under me by this disciple who insults you! Thus addressed, the son of Devarāta vomited the collection of *yajus* mantras;
then he departed, and the sages beheld those groups of *yajus* mantras.
The *yajus* verses, having become partridges (*tittiri*), delivered them out of a desire for them;
thus there arose the very elegant *Yajur-Veda* branch known as the Taittirīyas.
Then, O Brahmin, Yājñavalkya, seeking further knowledge of the Vedas (*chandas*), [proceeded].
While his teacher was away, he attended upon the Lord Āditya.
Śrī Yājñavalkya said:
"Oṃ, obeisances to the Blessed Āditya, who, as the very self of all the worlds, [is the form] of time..."
In Your own essential nature, You alone— unobstructed by limiting adjuncts like space both within the hearts and outside of the fourfold classes of beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—
withdraw the waters through a multitude of years accumulated by the divisions of moments, instants, and twilights.
By means of exhalation and inhalation, he sustains this worldly course.

O bull among the wise, O Savitṛ, that which shines there day after day at each pressing of the soma for those who worship according to the injunctions of the sacred tradition, [removes] all their sins and impurities.
We meditate upon the solar orb, the seed-roasting fire of the Lord,

which indeed impels here the groups of mind, senses, and vital breaths— which are non-self and whose true abode is the Lord— of all moving and stationary beings, acting as the inner controller of the Self.

He who, being supremely compassionate, beholding this world swallowed by the python-like seizure known as the darkness of most terrifying mouths—as if it were a lifeless corpse devoid of consciousness—raised it up by his mere glance, and day after day, at every juncture, established it in its own duty called *svadharma* for the sake of its ultimate welfare; ||| BhP_12.06.070/4 sa eva bhagavān asmat-kṛta-parādhasyāpi tava kṛpā-nidhir bhūtvā svātmānam darśayiṣyati. ||| that very Blessed One, becoming a treasury of mercy even toward you who have committed offenses against him, will reveal his own self. ||| BhP_12.06.070/5 tasmāt tvam api tam eva śaraṇam vraja. ||| Therefore, you too should go to him alone for refuge. ||| BhP_12.06.070/6 na hy anyat tat-pāda-mūla-śaraṇam gatānām iha janmani janmāntare vā jñāna-darśana-prāpti-vighnāya kalpate. ||| For nothing else can serve as an obstacle to the attainment of knowledge and vision for those who have gone for refuge to the soles of his feet, whether in this birth or in another birth. ||| BhP_12.06.070/7 yasya hi jñāna-darśana-prāptau vighno na jāyate sa vai mukta-gatiḥ. ||| Indeed, he for whom no obstacle arises in the attainment of knowledge and vision is one whose course is liberated. ||| BhP_12.06.070/8 tasmāt sarvathā bhagavantam eva śaraṇam vraja. ||| Therefore, in every way, go for refuge to the Blessed One alone. ||| BhP_12.06.070/9 sa hi sarveṣām bhūtānām ātma-bhūtaḥ. ||| For he is the Self of all beings. ||| BhP_12.06.070/10 sa eva hi sarva-bhūtāni dhārayati. ||| He alone indeed sustains all beings. ||| BhP_12.06.070/11 sa eva hi sarva-bhūtāni pālayati. ||| He alone indeed protects all beings. ||| BhP_12.06.070/12 sa eva hi sarva-bhūtāni saṃharati. ||| He alone indeed withdraws all beings. ||| BhP_12.06.070/13 sa eva hi sarva-bhūtāni sṛjati. ||| He alone indeed creates all beings. ||| BhP_12.06.070/14 sa eva hi sarva-bhūtāni praviśati. ||| He alone indeed enters into all beings. ||| BhP_12.06.070/15 sa eva hi sarva-bhūtāni vyāpnoti. ||| He alone indeed pervades all beings. ||| BhP_12.06.070/16 sa eva hi sarva-bhūtānām antaryāmī. ||| He alone indeed is the inner controller of all beings. ||| BhP_12.06.070/17 sa eva hi sarva-bhūtānām adhiṣṭhātā. ||| He alone indeed is the presiding lord of all beings. ||| BhP_12.06.070/18 sa eva hi sarva-bhūtānām śāstā. ||| He alone indeed is the teacher of all beings. ||| BhP_12.06.070/19 sa eva hi sarva-bhūtānām guruḥ. ||| He alone indeed is the preceptor of all beings. ||| BhP_12.06.070/20 sa eva hi sarva-bhūtānām pitā. ||| He alone indeed is the father of all beings. ||| BhP_12.06.070/
In this he acts appropriately;
like a sovereign king, he wanders everywhere, instilling fear in the wicked,
while being honored here and there by the guardians of the quarters with their hands folded like lotus buds in respectful salutation.
Sūta said: "Then, O Blessed One, desiring the *ayātayāma* (unwasted) *yajus* mantras, I approach Your pair of lotus feet, which are saluted by the teachers of the three worlds."

Thus praised and propitiated, the Blessed Lord Ravi, assuming the form of a horse, bestowed upon the sage the Yajus-mantras that had not yet lost their potency. By means of those Yajus-mantras, the omnipresent Lord composed fifteen branches (śākhās).
The Vājasaneyins, such as the Kāṇvas and Mādhyandinas, received them. From Jaimini, who was well-versed in the Sāman chants, there was a sage named Sumantu;
his son was Sutvan, who taught one *saṃhitā* each to those two lineages.

And Sukarmā, his disciple, who was a great tree for the Sāma Veda, then divided the Sāmans into a thousand *saṃhitās*, O twice-born one. Hiraṇyanābha of Kauśala and Pauṣyañji were the disciples of Sukarmā.
And another, the best among the knowers of Brahman, was Āvantya; he accepted two disciples.
There were indeed five hundred disciples from the north who were chanters of the Sāmans. They [the disciples] of Pauṣyañji and Āvantya are also declared to be Easterners (Prācya).
Laukāksi, Māṅgali, Kulya, Kuśīda, and Kukṣi,
as well as Pauṣyañji’s disciples, each received one hundred *saṃhitās*.
Of Hiraṇyanābha, there were twenty-four *saṃhitās* composed by Kṛta.
The disciple Śeṣa, who was self-controlled and a native of Āvanti, spoke to his own disciples.
Sūta said:
Then Sumantu, a knower of the Atharva Veda, instructed his own disciple.
He, in turn, taught the *Saṃhitā* to Pathya and Vedadarśa.
Śauklāyani, Brahmabali, Modoṣa, and Pippalāyani were the disciples of Vedadarśa; now hear of the disciples of Pathya.
O Brahmin, Kumuda, Śunaka, Jājali— who was also a knower of the Atharvaveda—
as well as Babhru, the disciple of Aṅgiras, and Saindhavāyana,
studied the two *saṃhitās*; likewise, others such as Sāvarṇa and his followers did so.
The Nakṣatrakalpa, the Śānti, Kaśyapa, Aṅgiras, and others—these are the teachers of the Atharvaveda; now hear, O sage, those who belong to the Purāṇas: Trayyāruṇi, Kaśyapa, Sāvarṇi, and Akṛtavraṇa.
Vaiśampāyana and Hārīta— these six were indeed the traditional reciters (paurāṇika) who studied the Saṃhitā from my father Vyāsa’s own mouth;
I, as their disciple, have mastered all of them, one by one.
"Kaśyapa, myself Sāvarṇi, Rāma’s disciple Akṛtavraṇa,
and [you]— these four disciples of Vyāsa studied the primary *Saṃhitās*.
O Brahman, the characteristics of the Purāṇas have been defined by the Brahmanical sages."
Listen with an attentive mind, in accordance with the Vedas and the scriptures:

[the topics are] creation (sarga), secondary creation (visarga), maintenance (vṛtti), protection (rakṣā), the intermediate periods (antarāṇi), genealogy (vaṃśa), the history of the lineage (vaṃśānucarita), dissolution (saṃsthā), the cause (hetu), and the refuge (apāśraya).
Those who know it declare that the Purāṇa is endowed with ten characteristics;

some, O Brahmin, consider it to be fivefold according to the distinction between the great and the small. From the unmanifest, through the agitation of the modes, arises the threefold mahat, and from that, the ego (ahaṃkāra).
The manifestation of the subtle elements, the senses, and their objects is called *sarga* (primary creation).
This *visarga* (secondary creation), consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), belongs to these [elements] as they are favored by the *puruṣa*.
It is a collection [of effects] where seed follows from seed, comprising all that is moving and unmoving.
The elements are the sustenance for all beings, both moving and non-moving;
among men, this was ordained by Him, whether through desire or by injunction.
O Acyuta, Your descent into the world is for the protection of the universe in age after age.

Among animals, mortals, sages, and gods, those who hate the three Vedas are slain by these [incarnations]. A Manvantara consists of the Manu, the gods, the sons of the Manu, the lords of the gods, the sages, and the partial incarnations (aṃśāvatāra) of Hari; thus it is said to be sixfold.

The lineage of kings born from Brahmā throughout the three periods of time, their genealogical history, their conduct, and those who maintained the dynasty; as well as the occasional dissolution, the elemental dissolution, the constant dissolution, and the absolute dissolution.
He is called "Saṃsthā" by the wise; by His own nature, He is fourfold.
The individual soul (jīva) is the cause of His creation and so forth, acting through ignorance and karma;
whom others call the "pervader" (anuśāyin) or the "undifferentiated" (avyākṛta).

That Brahman, which persists through presence and absence during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep— within those things composed of *māyā* and within the functions of the individual soul— is the ultimate refuge,
just as the substance "Being" alone persists amidst names and forms.

When the mind, having abandoned the three fluctuations by itself, ceases from its engagement with the five stages beginning with the seed and ending with dissolution— whether through yoga or otherwise—
then it turns away from this body and realizes the Self.

Thus, the sages who know the ancient lore have declared eighteen Purāṇas—both minor and major—characterized by their definitions and the subjects they describe. These are the Brāhma, Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Laiṅga, and Gāruḍa; [and further: the Mārkaṇḍeya, Āgneya, Bhaviṣyat, Brahmavaivarta, and Liṅga; the Varāha, Skānda, Vāmana, Kaurma, Matsya, and Sauram; and the Brahmanda and Bhāgavatam. Among these, the Bhāgavata is the best. It is the essence of all the Purāṇas, the supreme secret, and the ultimate goal of all the Vedas. It is the very life-breath of the Lord of Lakṣmī, the source of all happiness, and the most excellent among all scriptures. It is the supreme means for attaining the highest bliss.
