The Nāradīya, Bhāgavata, Āgneya, that which is named Skānda, the Bhaviṣya, Brahma-vaivarta, Mārkaṇḍeya along with the Vāmana,
the Vārāha, Mātsya, Kaurma, and the one called Brahmāṇḍa— these constitute the thirty-six [Purāṇas].
"O Brahmin, O Sage, this transmission of the branches by the sage has been fully described;
it increases the spiritual luster (*brahma-tejas*) of disciples, grand-disciples, and great-grand-disciples.
Śrī Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, live long, O virtuous one! Speak to us, O best among speakers.
For men wandering in the shoreless darkness, you are the one who shows the way across. People call the son of Mṛkaṇḍu a seer of long life.
He who remains at the end of the kalpa, by whom this entire world was swallowed— he,
that bull among the Bhṛgus, has indeed been born in our lineage during this very kalpa;
even now, no dissolution of beings whatsoever occurs.
While wandering alone upon the ocean, he reportedly beheld a single,
wondrous child lying within the hollow of a banyan leaf.
O Sūta, because of this, we have a great doubt and a deep curiosity.
"O great yogi, you who are honored even in the Purāṇas, please sever this doubt of ours.
Sūta said:
"O great sage, this question you have asked removes the delusion of the world."
Wherein the narrative of Nārāyaṇa is sung, which removes the impurities of the Kali age; Mārkaṇḍeya, having received the purificatory rites of the twice-born from his father in due order,
and having studied the Vedas according to dharma, was devoted to austerity and the study of sacred texts.
Observing the great vow, peaceful, with matted hair and clad in bark garments,
he carried a water-pot, a staff, a sacred thread, and a girdle,
as well as a black antelope skin, a rosary of beads, and *kuśa* grass, for the sake of fulfilling his religious observances.
Worshiping Hari during the two twilights in the fire, the sun, the guru, the brahmins, and his own self,
he would bring alms to his guru in the evening and morning; restrained in speech and permitted by his guru, he ate once, or otherwise remained fasting.
Thus, devoted to austerity and sacred study for ten billion years,
he worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa and conquered death, which is so difficult to overcome.
Brahmā, Bhṛgu, Bhava, Dakṣa, and the other sons of Brahmā—
Because of that, men, gods, ancestors, and living beings were filled with great wonder.
Thus, the yogi who observed the great vow meditated upon Adhokṣaja through austerity, Vedic study, and self-restraint, his inner self having destroyed all afflictions.
As that yogi was thus engaging his mind through great yoga,
a vast period of time consisting of six manvantaras passed away. Purandara, having learned of this, [acted] during this seventh interval.
O Brahmin, fearing his ascetic power, he began to obstruct it;
he dispatched the Gandharvas and Apsarases, as well as Spring, the Malaya breeze, Lust, and the intoxication born of passion, to the sage.
They went to that hermitage on the northern slope of the Himalayas,
O Lord, where the river Puṣpabhadrā flows and the stone named Citrā is situated. That holy site of the hermitage was adorned with sacred trees and creepers.

It was inhabited by holy families of twice-born brahmins; it possessed sacred and pure reservoirs of water; it resounded with the songs of intoxicated bees and the warbling of intoxicated cuckoos; it was filled with the majestic dancing of intoxicated peacocks and crowded with flocks of intoxicated birds.
The wind, having entered and taken up the spray from the snowy cascades, blew along,
embraced by *sumanaḥ* flowers, kindling the god of love;
it was like a night with a rising moon as its face, adorned with rows of coral clusters.
There, amidst the clusters of cowherds, trees, and creepers, was the spring season;
followed by hosts of Gandharvas with singing and instrumental music, Smara— the lord of the celestial women— was seen with his bow and arrows drawn.
The servants of Śakra saw him seated, having offered oblations into the fire; with eyes closed, he was invincible, like fire incarnate. Then women danced before him, and singers sang.
They played delightful music on mṛdaṅgas, vīṇās, and paṇavas. Then Kāma fixed his five-headed arrow upon his bow;
Madhu, the son of Rajas, and the servants of Indra caused them to tremble.
As Puñjikasthalī played with balls, her waist became deeply distressed by the weight of her breasts; her garlands fell from her loosened hair as she moved here and there,
her gaze following the ball.
The wind blew away her garment, which was fine and whose girdle had snapped;
then Smara discharged his arrow, thinking him already conquered by himself. But everything there became futile, like the effort of one who lacks mastery.

O sage, although thus harassed by the followers of Indra, the great sage— withdrawing like young children who have awakened a sleeping serpent— returned home, being scorched by the power of that muni’s splendor as they committed such offenses.
O Brahmin, even though the great sage was thus provoked by Indra’s attendants...
That I have attained a state free from pride is not surprising, for such is the nature of the great;
yet, having seen Kāma along with his host rendered powerless,
and having heard of the spiritual power of the Brahman-sage, the Lord, the self-ruling Sovereign, was filled with supreme wonder.
As he was thus engaging his mind through austerity, Vedic study, and self-restraint,
Hari appeared in the form of Nara and Nārāyaṇa to bestow His grace upon him.
They were white and dark, with eyes like fresh lotuses.
They had four arms and wore garments of deerskin and bark;
their hands held the sacred grass (pavitra), and they bore the three-stranded sacrificial thread (upavīta), a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), and a straight staff made of bamboo.
A rosary of lotus seeds, a water-purifying vessel,
and the Veda— these three were manifest as the very forms of austerity itself,
glowing with a tawny radiance like the color of a blazing lightning bolt.
Those two, who were tall and honored by the best of the gods,
were indeed the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the forms of the Blessed Lord;
seeing them, he rose up with reverence and bowed down with his body like a staff.
With his soul, senses, and inner being satisfied by the bliss of that vision,
his hair standing on end and his eyes filled with tears, he could not bear to look at them;
rising up with palms joined in reverence, he bowed low as if wishing to embrace them out of longing.
"Obeisances, obeisances!"— thus the two lords spoke with faltering words. Taking seats for them and washing their feet,
he worshiped them with offerings, ointments, incense, and garlands.
Seated comfortably on their seats, the two sages were disposed toward grace;
bowing again at their feet, he spoke thus to those most venerable ones.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O All-pervading Lord, how can I describe You?
For when Your breath is uttered, the vital breath vibrates; following that, the speech, mind, and senses of embodied beings, as well as those of Aja and Śarva, indeed begin to move.
Moreover, You are the kinsman of the hearts of those who worship You, even of Yourself.
O Blessed One, these two forms of the Lord are for the welfare of the three worlds,
for the cessation of suffering, and for victory over death.
You assume various other bodies in order to protect this world, just as a spider emits and then again swallows everything;
[I take refuge] in the soles of the feet of that Protector and Lord of all moving and stationary beings.
Those situated in whom neither karma, nor the qualities of nature (*guṇa*), nor the passion of time (*kāla-rajas*) touch;
whom the sages— whose very hearts are the Vedas— constantly praise, bow down to, worship, and meditate upon for the sake of attaining that [state].

O Lord, we know of no other source of security for a person beset by fear on all sides than taking refuge at Your feet, which are the very embodiment of liberation; even Brahmā, who occupies a throne for two *parārdhas*, is utterly afraid of this [cycle of birth and death].
What need is there to speak of Time or of the material elements created by it?
O You of truthful intellect, I indeed take refuge at the soles of Your feet,
having abandoned this covering of the self belonging to the Supreme Teacher of the soul.
The body and so forth are useless, unreal, and perishable; one should realize that You alone are the pure conscious Knower.
Then, O Lord, all desired objects will be attained by you.
O Master, the qualities of goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas) are merely bonds for Your own Self.
The causes of this world's maintenance, dissolution, and emergence consist of His illusory energies (māyā); yet,
He also assumes forms composed of pure goodness (sattva) as His divine play (līlā) for the sake of peace,
for these other forms do not remove the calamities, delusions, and fears of men.
Therefore, O Blessed One, here in this world, those who are skilled worship Your pure form, which is dear to You; for the Sātvatas desire that sattva which is Your very nature as the Supreme Person.

Salutations to that Blessed One, the Supreme Person, the Infinite, the All-pervading, the Teacher of the universe, and the Supreme Deity— from whom the world attains fearlessness and the bliss of the Self, and from no other.
Salutations to Nārāyaṇa, the seer, the supreme among men,
the swan-like one of restrained speech, the Lord of the Vedas; whom indeed those of wandering intellect do not know through the paths of the false senses.
Though he was present among his own vital breaths, in his heart, and even within the range of his vision,
his intelligence was veiled by Your illusory power (māyā); yet, having approached You— the primordial source and teacher of all— he directly received the Veda.
The vision of whom is the secret revelation of the Self disclosed by the Vedas;
wherein even the wise, though striving with effort directed toward the Unborn, are bewildered—
he whose character conforms to the scope of all philosophical doctrines.
"I bow to the Great Person, whose consciousness is hidden within the self.
Sūta said:
Thus was the Blessed One praised by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya.
Nārāyaṇa, the friend of Nara, being pleased, spoke to the descendant of Bhṛgu. The Blessed Lord said:
"O, O best of brahminical sages, you have attained perfection through self-concentration."
"By means of unswerving devotion to Me, through austerity, Vedic study, and self-restraint,
and by your performance of this great vow, we have been thoroughly pleased. Choose a boon— blessings upon you— for I am the giver of boons desired by you."
The venerable sage said:
"Victory to you, O Lord of the gods of gods! O Acyuta, who removes the suffering of those who have sought refuge! Enough for us with this much of a boon—that you have been beheld by us."

Having attained the vision of your glorious lotus feet through a mind ripened by yoga, Brahmā and the other gods have become like that to me; yet, O lotus-petal-eyed one, crest-jewel of those of meritorious fame, you have now come within the range of my eyes.
"I shall behold the Māyā by which the world, along with its protectors, perceives the difference between the Real and the unreal.
Sūta said:
"O sage, having been thus praised and worshipped according to his desire by the Ṛṣi, the Blessed One..."
Saying "So be it," the Lord smiled and departed for Badarikāśrama;
meanwhile, the sage remained in his own hermitage, contemplating that very matter,
dwelling within fire, sun, moon, water, earth, air, ether, and the self.
Meditating on Hari everywhere, he worshipped Him with offerings of his inner disposition; at times, overwhelmed by the surging flow of love, he forgot the ritual worship itself.
O best of sages, once, on the bank of the Puṣpabhadrā river, that sage—
O Brahmin, as he was performing his twilight devotions, a great wind arose;
and as it emitted a fierce sound, formidable clouds gathered around it,
discharging torrents of rain along with massive hailstones and flashing lightning that roared loudly.
Then the four oceans appeared on all sides, swallowing the surface of the earth,
with fierce waves driven by the wind, possessing formidable crocodiles and deep-sounding whirlpools;
they were filled with waters that surpassed the heavens in brilliance both within and without.
Seeing the fourfold world, including himself, tormented by the lightning bolts,
and the earth submerged in water, the sage became despondent and was filled with fear.
As he was looking on in this manner, the great ocean— terrifying with its waves, its waters churned by violent winds,
and being filled by raining clouds— submerged the earth along with its continents, regions, and mountains,
as well as the atmosphere, the heavens, and the hosts of celestial beings.
The three worlds, along with the cardinal directions, were submerged;
that great sage alone remained,
wandering about with his matted locks disheveled like one who is dull-witted and blind.
Overcome by hunger and thirst, harassed by crocodiles and *timiṅgila* fish, struck by waves and winds,
he fell into shoreless darkness, wandering through the directions.
Driven by exhaustion, he does not perceive the sky or the earth;
sometimes submerged in a great whirlpool, he is struck by turbulent waves;
and in other places, he is devoured by aquatic creatures that strike one another.
In some places he encounters grief, in some delusion, in some suffering, happiness, or fear;
and in some places, afflicted by diseases and the like, he meets with death. This continues for tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands, and millions of years.

As he wandered there, his mind enveloped by the illusory power (*māyā*) of Viṣṇu, many years passed. Once, while wandering upon that summit of the earth, the twice-born one beheld a young banyan tree, adorned with fruits and tender sprouts.
On its north-eastern branch, he also beheld a child lying in a leaf-cup, swallowing the darkness with his radiance—
a child dark as a great emerald, with a beautiful lotus-face.

With a neck like a conch-shell, a broad chest, a beautiful nose, and lovely eyebrows; with locks of hair shimmering as they quiver with his breath, and ears adorned with pomegranates that possess the splendor of a conch-shell;
with a smile of nectar that appears slightly reddened by the luster of his coral-like lips.

With his lotus-like feet— whose outer corners were as red as the interior of a lotus, whose heart-stealing smiles and glances were directed toward him, and whose deep navel and petal-like abdomen were slightly agitated by the movement of his breath— he lifted them up with his two hands, which possessed beautiful fingers.
Placing [the child] in his mouth, the best of Brahmins, seeing him sucking, was struck with wonder.
From that sight, his fatigue vanished; with joy, the lotus of his heart and his lotus-eyes blossomed wide.
With his hair standing on end and filled with a sense of amazement and apprehension, he stepped forward toward the boy to question him.
At that moment, by the mere breath of the child, O Bhārgava,
he entered into the interior of the body like a mosquito; there too,
he beheld everything placed within in its entirety.
Just as before, he was utterly amazed and bewildered by the sky,
the earth and heavens, the hosts of stars, the mountains and oceans, the islands with their regions, the cardinal directions, the gods and demons,
the forests, countries, rivers, cities, towns, villages, hermitages, and the duties of the various social orders.
Then he beheld the great elements and their elemental derivatives, as well as time and the various arrangements of ages and kalpas;
whatever else is a cause for worldly transaction, the entire universe appearing as if real.
He saw the Himālaya, that flower-bearing river, and his own hermitage where the sages resided.

Beholding the entire universe being expelled from the breath of the Child, he fell into the ocean of dissolution; there he beheld the banyan tree grown upon the summit of the earth, and the Child lying within the fold of its leaf,
gazing at him with side-long glances and the nectar of a smile born of parental love.
Then, beholding that child established within his heart with his two eyes, he, being deeply distressed, approached Adhokṣaja to embrace him; at that moment,
the Blessed Lord himself, the master of yoga dwelling in the cave of the heart, appeared.
O sage, it vanished instantly, just as the destruction of this world created by the Unruler [had appeared]; then, O Brahmin, the flood of waters that had submerged the world followed him,
but in a moment it disappeared from his hermitage, and he remained there as before.
Sūta said:
Having thus experienced this manifestation of the power of Yoga-māyā created by Nārāyaṇa, he went for refuge to Him alone.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Hari, I have taken refuge at the soles of Your feet, which grant fearlessness to those who seek refuge;
for even the gods are bewildered by Your māyā, despite their illumination of knowledge.
Sūta said:
While wandering through the heavens on his bull,
the Lord Rudra, surrounded by his own attendants, beheld him whose self was thus composed, together with Rudrāṇī.
Then Umā, beholding that sage, addressed Giriśa:
"O Blessed One, behold this brahmin, whose self, senses, and mind are perfectly stilled,
like the ocean when the wind has ceased and its multitude of fish and turtles are motionless."
"O bestower of perfection, you shall personally grant the complete success of this penance.
The Blessed Lord said:
"This brahminical sage desires no blessings whatsoever, not even liberation."
He has attained supreme devotion for the imperishable Lord, the Supreme Person;
nevertheless, we shall converse with this virtuous man,
for association with the saintly is the highest gain for human beings.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the refuge of the virtuous, the Lord of all branches of knowledge and the Sovereign of all embodied beings, approached him.

He did not perceive the arrival of those two, the Lords who are the Self of the universe, nor himself, nor the entire world, for the functions of his intellect were obstructed. The Blessed Lord Giriśa, perceiving that, [acted] through his yogic power (yoga-māyā).
The Lord entered the space within his cave like the wind entering a hollow;
he had attained auspiciousness within himself, wearing matted hair tawny as lightning,
possessing three eyes and ten arms, tall and rising like the sun.

Seeing him suddenly manifest in his heart, wearing a tiger-skin garment and bearing a trident, a bow, arrows, a sword, a shield, a rosary, a hand-drum, a skull-bowl, and an axe, he was struck with wonder.

"What is this, and from where does it come?"— having thus ceased from his meditative absorption, the sage opened his eyes and beheld Rudra, the sole preceptor of the three worlds, accompanied by his attendants at the Soma sacrifice; the sage then bowed his head to him.
To him and his attendants, together with Umā,
he offered worship with welcome, a seat, water for the feet, the arghya offering, perfumes, garlands, incense, and lamps.
Then, by virtue of his own spiritual power, he spoke to the Lord, whose every desire was already fulfilled:
O Lord, what can we do by which this world may find peace? Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful, the pure essence (*sattva*), and the one who bestows joy;
salutations to You who delight in passion (*rajas*), the terrible one, and the one who delights in darkness (*tamas*).
Sūta said:
Thus praised, the Blessed Lord, the primordial God and refuge of the virtuous,
being thoroughly satisfied and gracious in soul, spoke to him with a smile.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Choose a boon from us; we three are givers of boons. For mortals who obtain the sight of us, that vision is never in vain, as they thereby attain immortality."
Virtuous brāhmaṇas— peaceful, free from attachment, compassionate toward all beings,
solely devoted to Me, devoid of enmity, and possessing equal vision—
even the inhabitants of the worlds along with their guardians bow down to them, worship them, and serve them.

I, the Blessed Brahmā, and Hari himself, the Lord—none of us perceive even the slightest difference between you, Acyuta, and the Unborn (Aja). Nor do we perceive any difference between ourselves and the people; therefore, we honor you all equally.
For holy places do not consist of water, nor do the gods exist apart from consciousness;
they purify only after a long time, whereas you purify by the mere sight of you.
We offer our obeisances to the brāhmaṇas, who possess a form composed of the three Vedas just like ours.
By maintaining self-concentration, austerity, Vedic study, and self-restraint,
even those who have committed great sins would be purified by hearing of you or seeing you; how much more so, then, for those born of the lowest castes through conversation and other such means?
Sūta said:
Thus, drinking with his ears the nectar-like words of the one who has the moon as his crest-ornament— words augmented by the secrets of dharma— the sage was not satiated.
Having been long deluded by the illusory power (*māyā*) of Viṣṇu and greatly emaciated,
his mass of afflictions destroyed by the nectar of Śiva’s words, he spoke to him.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Oh, how inconceivable to embodied beings is this divine play of the Lord,
that those who are themselves objects of worship and the masters of the world bow down and offer praise! Indeed,
it is for the sake of making embodied beings grasp the path of righteousness that the speakers of the scriptures generally act in such a manner.
They practice [these deeds], approve of them when they are being performed, and praise them;
yet by such means— the activities consisting of the Lord’s own *māyā*— the power of the Blessed One is not defiled by them, just as a magician is not tainted by his own illusions.
Salutations to that Blessed Lord, who, having created this universe by His mind and entered it with His own self,
appears as if He were the agent through the functioning modes of nature, just like one who observes a dream.
Salutations to Him, the Supreme Lord, who possesses the three modes and whose very nature is the modes.

O Infinite One, what supreme boon could I possibly choose from You, the bestower of boons, after beholding You— the absolute, non-dual Guru who is the very embodiment of Brahman? For by the sight of You, a person becomes one whose desires are fulfilled and whose will is realized in truth.
"Nevertheless, I choose one boon from You who rain down the fulfillment of all desires:
unwavering devotion to the Blessed One, as well as to those devoted to Him, and likewise to You.
Sūta said:
Thus honored and praised by the sage with well-spoken words, the Blessed Lord Śarva, together with Śarvī, greeted him and said:
"O great seer, this desire of yours is fulfilled; you are entirely devoted to Adhokṣaja."

O Brahman, until the end of the kalpa, may you possess fame, merit, freedom from old age and death, as well as knowledge of the three periods of time, realized wisdom, and detachment; may you be endowed with Vedic splendor, and may you become a teacher of the Purāṇas.
Sūta said:
Having thus granted those boons to the sage, the three-eyed Lord departed,
recounting to the Goddess that deed which he had previously experienced with him.

That best of the Bhṛgus, having attained the greatness of supreme yoga, even now wanders about, truly established in exclusive devotion to Hari. Thus has the story of the wise Mārkaṇḍeya been described to you.

Some who lack true knowledge declare that this wonderful display of the Lord’s illusory power (*māyā-vaibhava*), which has been experienced by them, is merely the beginningless cycle of worldly existence for the self,
occurring only occasionally for human beings.

O best of the Bhṛgus, both he who narrates and he who hears this account of the majesty of the Discus-wielder as it has been described— neither of them shall experience the cycle of rebirth resulting from the accumulation of karma. Śrī Śaunaka said:
Now we ask this matter of you, who are most wealthy in knowledge:
you are the knower of the truth of the Bhāgavata in the final conclusions of all the tantras.
The followers of the Tantras [engage] in the service of the Lord of Śrī alone.
Describe to us— may you be blessed— the manner and the means by which they fashion His limbs, secondary members, weapons, and ornaments; for we desire to know this *kriyā-yoga*,
by which skill in action a mortal may attain immortality.
Sūta said:
Having paid homage to my teachers, I shall describe the Vaiṣṇava manifestations (vibhūtis),
which have been proclaimed by the masters beginning with Brahmā, according to both the Vedas and the Tantras.
The Virāṭ, composed of transformations and consisting of the nine principles beginning with Māyā, is seen therein; within that conscious [Virāṭ], the three worlds are manifested.
This indeed is the form of the Supreme Person (Puruṣa): the earth is His feet, and the heavens are His head; the sky is His chest.
The sun is the navel of the Lord, the wind is his two nostrils, and the quarters of space are his two ears.
Prajāpati is the organ of generation of the Ruler, and death is his downward breath (apāna). The world-protectors are his arms, the moon is his mind, and Yama is his eyebrows.
His lower lip is supreme modesty, greed is his teeth, and his smile is the moonlight;
his body hair is the trees, and the clouds are the hair upon the head of that All-pervading One. Indeed, in whatever measure this Puruṣa is defined by whatever form, [so is He].
That Great Person, the Unborn, likewise maintains His own self-effulgence under the designation of the *kaustubha* gem according to the worldly convention;
its pervasive radiance is itself the Śrīvatsa mark which the All-pervading Lord bears upon His chest.
Wearing His own *māyā*, known as the forest garland (*vana-mālā*), which consists of manifold qualities;

wearing yellow garments composed of the Vedas (*chandas*); wearing the sacred thread (*brahma-sūtra*) consisting of the threefold Vedic accents (*svara*); and wearing earrings in the shape of sea-monsters (*makara*) representing *sāṅkhya* and *yoga*, the Lord bears these [ornaments].
The crown is the station of supreme sovereignty that grants fearlessness to all worlds;
the seat presided over by Him is called the Unmanifest (avyākṛta) and Infinite (ananta).
Here, the lotus is said to be the quality of goodness (sattva), endowed with righteousness, knowledge, and other virtues.
Holding a mace, he who possesses *ojas*, *sahas*, and *bala* is the primary principle (*mukhya-tattva*);
the conch is the principle of water (*apām tattva*), the excellent discus is the principle of fire (*tejas-tattva*),
the sword resembling the sky is the principle of ether (*nabhas-tattva*), and the shield consists of the quality of darkness (*tamas*).
They say that Time is his form, the Śārṅga bow is made of karma,
and the arrows are the senses; his chariot is intention (ākūti),
while the subtle elements (tanmātras) are its manifestation through the nature of purposeful action.
The sacred circle is the place for worshiping the gods, and initiation is the purification of the self. Service to the Blessed One is the destruction of one's own sins.
The Blessed One bears the lotus of his divine play, which is the very meaning of the word *bhaga*.

The Lord attended to his righteousness and fame with two fly-whisks, while Vaikuṇṭha held the parasol; O twice-born ones, that abode is free from all fear. The threefold Veda, known as Suparṇa, carries the Person (Puruṣa) in the sacrifice.
The goddess Śrī is the inseparable consort of the Lord Hari himself;

Viṣvakṣena is known as the personification of His administration and the chief of His attendants; and Nanda and the other seven are the eight doorkeepers, who are the very powers of Hari’s attributes, such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
O Brahmin, Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Puruṣa himself— Aniruddha— is designated as the expansion of forms (mūrti-vyūha).
He is known by his functions as Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and Turīya.
The Lord is contemplated through the knowledge of objects, the senses,
and the internal disposition; the Lord Hari, the Sovereign, possessing four forms, bears those four [aspects] through his limbs, secondary limbs, weapons, and ornaments.
O best of the twice-born, He is the source of Brahman, self-perceiving,
and fully complete in His own majesty; by His own *māyā*, He creates, maintains, and withdraws this universe, His vision being unobstructed by these designations.

O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, friend of Kṛṣṇa, bull among the Vṛṣṇis, enemy of the mountains, whose prowess is inexhaustible as it consumes the dynasties of kings— You are revealed by those devoted to You as the very Self to be attained; thus has it been declared.
O Govinda, whose fame as a holy place is auspicious to hear, you who are sung of by the cowherd women, the cowherds, and your servants— protect your servants!
He who, having risen at dawn, recites this description of the characteristics of the Great Person...
With his mind fixed on that and being self-restrained, he should mutter the Veda which dwells within the cave of the heart.
Śrī Śaunaka said:
[Tell us] what the venerable Śuka spoke to Viṣṇurāta as he listened.

In every month, a group of seven belonging to Sūrya resides in various forms. Tell us— who are full of faith— the names and duties of those appointed by their lords, and the manifestation of Hari in his solar form.
Sūta said:
By means of beginningless ignorance regarding Viṣṇu, the Self of all embodied beings,
this cosmic order has been fashioned and revolves within the worlds.
Hari alone is the sun of the worlds, the creator of the self and all else;
he is the root of all Vedic rituals, proclaimed in many ways by the seers.
Time, place, action, the agent, the instrument, the effect, and the scripture—[all these are rooted in him].
O Brahman, Hari is said to be unconquerable through the ninefold offering of substances and fruits.
In the twelve months beginning with Madhu, the Blessed Lord, assuming the form of Time,
moves for the governance of the world through twelve distinct groups.
O sage, Dhātṛ, Kṛtasthalī, Heti, Vāsuki, Rathakṛt,
Pulastya, and Tumburu— these carry away the month of Madhu.
Aryaman, Pulaha, Ojas, Praheti, and Puñjikasthalī [carry away the month of Mādhava].
Nārada, Kacchanīra,
Mitra, Atri, Pauruṣeya, Takṣaka, Menakā, Hāhā,
and Rathasvana— these indeed lead Mādhava through the month of Śukra.

Vasiṣṭha, Varuṇa, Rambhā, Sahajanya, and Huhū, as well as Śukra and Citrasvana— these carry the month of Śuci (Jyeṣṭha). Indra, Viśvāvasu, Śrotā, Elāpatra, and likewise Aṅgiras [carry the month of Āṣāḍha].
Pramlocā, the excellent Rākṣasa, and these others lead the month of Nabhas; Vivasvān, Ugrasena, Vyāghra, Āsāraṇa, and Bhṛgu,
along with Anumlocā and Śaṅkhapāla, lead the month known as Nabhasya.
Pūṣan, Dhanañjaya, Vāta, Suṣeṇa, and likewise Suruci,
as well as Ghṛtācī and Gautama— these carry the month of Tapas.
Ṛtu, Varcas, Bharadvāja, Parjanya, and likewise Senajit [carry the month of Tapaḥ-saṃyukta].
Viśva and Airāvata— these lead the period known as Tapas.
Furthermore, Aṃśu, Kaśyapa, Tārkṣya, Ṛtasena, Urvaśī, Vidyucchatru, Mahāśaṅkha, and Sahas— these lead the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Bhaga, Sphūrja, Ariṣṭanemi, Ūrṇa, and Āyu as the fifth;
Karkoṭaka and Pūrvacitti—these lead the month of Puṣya. Tvaṣṭṛ, the son of Ṛcīka, Kambala, and Tilottamā.
Brahmāpeta, Satyajit, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Iṣambharas;
Viṣṇu, Aśvatara, Rambhā, Sūryavarcas, and Satyajit; Viśvāmitra and Makhāpeta—these lead the month of Ūrja.
These are the manifestations of the Blessed Viṣṇu Āditya;
for men who remember them at the two junctions of the day (saṃdhyā), they take away their sin day by day.
Indeed, throughout all twelve months, this Lord [is present] with six [of these forms].
Moving everywhere, he extends right understanding both in this world and in the hereafter.
The seers praise him with the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajur Vedas characterized by his own marks;
the Gandharvas sing of him, and the Apsarases dance before him.

The elephants, the village chiefs, and the chariot-yokers harnessed the chariot; the powerful Nairṛtas urged it on from behind. Sixty thousand stainless Brahman-sages, the Vālakhilyas, [also attended].
They go before Him, facing Him, and praise the All-pervading Lord with hymns of praise.
For thus the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign, who is without beginning or end, protects the worlds by manifesting His own self in every kalpa, O Unborn One.
Sūta said:
Salutations to the Great Dharma; salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the Creator.
Having offered obeisance to the knowers of Brahman, I shall declare the eternal dharmas.
O brāhmaṇas, this wonderful account of Viṣṇu has been narrated to you,
as requested by you regarding that which is appropriate for men.
In this, Hari himself, the remover of all sins, has been glorified.
Nārāyaṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Blessed Lord, the Master of the Sātvatas—
herein has been declared the supreme Brahman, the secret of the origin and dissolution of the universe, as well as the knowledge concerning Him, together with realized wisdom (vijñāna).
Devotional yoga (bhakti-yoga) has been fully described, along with detachment (vairāgya) which rests upon it;
as well as the narrative concerning Parīkṣit and the account related by Nārada.
Furthermore, there is the account of the royal sage Parīkṣit’s fasting unto death following the curse of a brāhmaṇa.
The dialogue between Śuka, the bull among Brahmins, and Parīkṣit; the departure [of Śuka] by means of yogic concentration (yoga-dhāraṇā); the dialogue between Nārada and Ajamīḍha;
the Avatārānugīta; and first, the creation pertaining to Pradhāna.
The dialogue between Vidura and Uddhava; then the conversation between Kṣattṛ and Maitreya; the inquiry regarding the Purāṇa-saṃhitā; the manifestation of the Mahāpuruṣa;
and then the primary (prākṛtika) creation as well as the seven secondary (vaikṛtika) creations.
From that [lotus] arose the birth of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), from which the Vairāja Puruṣa was born; there,
the movement of both gross and subtle time occurred,
and the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa took place during the lifting of the earth from the ocean.
The creation of those above, across, and below, as well as the creation of Rudra,
and then that of Ardhanārīśvara, from whom Svāyambhuva Manu [arose],
and Śatarūpā, who was the first and most excellent of women; [all these arose from him].
The lineage of the lawful wives of the patriarch Kardama; the descent of the exalted and great-souled Lord Kapila;
and the dialogue between Devahūtī and the wise Kapila.

The origin of the nine Brahmās, the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the life-story of Dhruva, and thereafter that of Pṛthu Prācīnabarhiṣ; then the dialogue with Nārada, O twice-born ones, and then the account of Praiyavrata.
Then follows the account of Nābhi, as well as that of Ṛṣabha and Bharata;
a description of the islands, regions, and oceans, along with their mountains and rivers; the configuration of the celestial sphere; and the arrangement of the subterranean realms and hells.
The birth of Dakṣa from the Pracetasas and the progeny of their daughters,
from whom sprang the gods, asuras, humans, animals, serpents, birds, and so forth;
and the birth and death of the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, O twice-born ones, as well as that of the two sons of Diti.
The life-story of Prahlāda, the high-souled lord of the Daityas; the narration of the Manvantaras; the liberation of Gajendra;
and the incarnations of Viṣṇu during the Manvantaras, such as Hayagrīva and others.
The incarnations of the Lord of the universe as the Tortoise, the Fish, the Man-lion, and the Dwarf;
likewise, the churning of the Ocean of Milk for the sake of the nectar of the gods;
the great battle between the gods and the asuras; and the glorification of the royal dynasties.

The birth of Ikṣvāku and his lineage, the account of the high-souled Sudyumna, the story of Ilā and the story of Tārā are told here; as well as the narration of the Solar dynasty, beginning with Śaśāda, Nṛga, and others.
The sin-destroying life stories of Saucanya, Śaryāti, and the wise Kakutstha; of Khaṭvāṅga, Māndhātṛ, Saubhari, and Sagara; and of Rāma, the lord of Kośala.
The renunciation of his body by Nimi, the birth of the Janakas,
the purification of the earth from the kṣatriyas by Rāma, the lord of the Bhṛgus, and [the histories] of Aila, of the Lunar dynasty, of Yayāti, and of Nahuṣa.
The lineage of Bharata, son of Duṣmanta; of Śāntanu and his son;
and of Yadu, the eldest son of Yayāti, has been proclaimed—the lineage in which the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of the Universe, known as Kṛṣṇa, descended.
His birth in the house of Vasudeva and his subsequent growth in Gokula have been described;
the boundless deeds of that enemy of the asuras have been proclaimed,
such as the infant’s drinking of Pūtanā’s breast-milk and the overturning of the cart.
The crushing of Tṛṇāvarta, as well as that of Baka and Vatsa;
the slaying of Aghāsura by the Creator, and the embracing of the calves and cowherds;
the destruction of Dhenuka along with his brother Pralamba.
The protection of the cowherds as a forest fire crept toward them; the subduing of the serpent Kāliya, the great snake; the liberation of Nanda;
and the practice of vows by the maidens, wherein Acyuta was pleased by their observances.
The favor shown to the wives of the sacrificers and the consolation of the brāhmaṇas; the lifting of Govardhana Hill, and then the honoring of Indra and Surabhi;
the ceremonial bath for Kṛṣṇa at the sacrifice, and His sporting with the women during the nights.
The slaying of the evil-minded Śaṅkhacūḍa, Ariṣṭa, and Keśin; thereafter, the arrival of Akrūra, the departure of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
the lamentation of the women of Vraja, and then the sight of Mathurā.
The slaying of Gaja, Muṣṭika, Cāṇūra, Kaṃsa, and others;
likewise, the bringing back of the deceased son of his preceptor Sāndīpani;
and whatever was pleasing to the host of Yadus while he resided in Mathurā.
O twice-born ones, Hari, joined by Uddhava and Rāma,
performed the repeated slaughter of the army brought together by Jarāsaṃdha,
the slaying of the lord of the Yavanas, and the founding of Kuśasthalī.
The taking of the *pārijāta* tree from the abode of the gods along with the hall of Sudharmā;
the abduction of Rukmiṇī by Hari after crushing his enemies in battle; and the yawning of Hara in battle and the severing of Bāṇa’s arms.
Having slain the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa and carried away his daughters;
and [having slain] the wicked-minded Caidya, Pauṇḍraka, Śālva, Dantavakra,
Śambara, Dvivida, Pīṭha, Mura, Pañcajana, and others.
The majesty of their slaughter and the burning of Vārāṇasī,
the removal of the earth's burden by means of the Pāṇḍavas,
and the destruction of his own family under the pretext of the brahmins' curse.
The wonderful dialogue between Uddhava and Vasudeva,
wherein the entire science of the Self (*ātma-vidyā*) and the definitive determination of dharma were proclaimed;
and thereafter, the renunciation of the mortal body through the power of self-realization (*ātma-yoga*).
The characteristics and functions of the Yugas, the calamities of men in the Kali age, the fourfold dissolution, the threefold creation,
and the abandonment of the body by the wise royal sage Viṣṇurāta.

O best of the twice-born, I have thus related to you that which I was asked here: the transmission of the branches [of the Veda] by the sage Mārkaṇḍeya, his sacred narrative, and the manifestation of the Great Person, the Sun who is the soul of the universe.
The deeds performed during his playful incarnations have been recounted here in their entirety.
Even one who has fallen, stumbled, is afflicted by distress, or is overcome by hunger, if he involuntarily utters "Obeisance to Hari! aloud, he is liberated from all sins.

When the infinite Lord is glorified, His power having been heard, He indeed enters the hearts of men and shakes off their afflictions entirely—just as the sun dispels darkness or a strong wind scatters the clouds.
Those words which do not recount the Blessed One, the Transcendent (Adhokṣaja), are false; for they are untruthful and are merely the talk of the wicked.
That alone is truth; that indeed is auspiciousness; that alone is merit arising from the qualities of the Blessed Lord.
That alone is delightful, beautiful, and ever-new; that alone is the perpetual great festival for the mind.
That alone dries up the ocean of sorrow for men—that which is sung as the glory of the One of Excellent Renown.
That speech which never proclaims the fame of Hari— which purifies the world— even if it contains wonderful words,
is a watering hole for crows and not frequented by swans.
Where Acyuta is, there indeed are the stainless saintly persons.

That utterance of speech which, even if it be uncomposed verse by verse, is marked by the fame of the Infinite One— those saintly persons who hear, sing, and praise those names therein cause the flood of sins of the people to subside.
Even the state of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya*), if devoid of devotion to Acyuta,
does not shine, much less the stainless knowledge (*jñāna*);
how much less so that which is eternally inauspicious toward the Lord?
For even the most excellent action, when not offered [to Him],

is merely a supreme exertion for the sake of fame and prosperity; whereas the non-forgetfulness of the lotus feet of Śrīdhara arises from devotion to hearing the recitation of His qualities and other such practices, including the conduct, austerity, and scriptural study prescribed for one’s social class and stage of life.
The non-forgetfulness of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet destroys all that is inauspicious and extends well-being;
it brings about the purification of the mind, devotion to the Supreme Self, and knowledge coupled with realized wisdom and detachment.
O best of the twice-born, you are indeed most fortunate, for you constantly perceive Him who is the Self of all within your own selves.
Those of eternal nature, having taken refuge in the Lord Nārāyaṇa— the God who is beyond the gods, the Sovereign—

entered into Him. And I too was reminded of the reality of the Self, which I had previously heard from the mouth of the supreme Ṛṣi while King Parīkṣit was fasting unto death and the great sages were listening.
O Brahmins, this greatness of Vāsudeva, whose deeds are vast and worthy of being told, has been narrated to you; it is the destroyer of all inauspiciousness.
He who, with a mind focused on no other, should constantly cause this to be heard, even for a single watch or moment—

Whether one listens with faith to a single verse, half a verse, a quarter, or even half a quarter, such a person purifies their very self. By listening on the twelfth or the eleventh lunar day, one becomes endowed with long life.
One who, being self-restrained and fasting, recites this [text] becomes purified from sin; likewise,
one who is self-controlled, having fasted at Puṣkara, Mathurā, or Dvāravatī and recited this *saṃhitā*, is liberated from fear.
Deities, sages, perfected beings, ancestors, Manus,
and kings grant all desires to one who chants or hears the glorification of Him.
Having studied the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, the twice-born attains his goals through Him.
The fruit of that is streams of honey, streams of clarified butter, and streams of milk.
Having studied this Purāṇic compendium with self-restraint,
a twice-born man shall go to that supreme abode which was described by the Blessed Lord.
By studying this, a Brahmin shall attain wisdom; a Kṣatriya shall obtain the earth girt by the oceans;
a Vaiśya shall become a lord of treasures; and a Śūdra shall be purified from sin.
Indeed, Hari, the Lord of all who destroys the accumulation of the impurities of the Kali age, is not constantly glorified elsewhere.

But here, moreover, the Blessed One, whose form is the entirety of all things, has been described step by step through the course of these narrations. To Him— I bow down to that Acyuta, the unborn and infinite, the reality of the Self, whose own power constitutes the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, and whose praises are difficult even for the lords of heaven, such as Brahmā, Indra, and Śaṅkara, to fully comprehend.

Salutations to the eternal Lord, the bull among gods, whose nature is the mere perception [of Himself], who has constructed within His own self the abodes of both the stationary and the moving through His accumulated ninefold potencies,
and whose mind is composed in His own bliss, having cast aside all other states of being.
I bow to that son of Vyāsa, who, his heart drawn by the unconquerable and charming pastimes of the Lord, compassionately composed this Purāṇa which is a lamp of truth and destroys all sins.
Sūta said:
He whom Brahmā, Varuṇa, Indra, Rudra, and the Maruts praise with divine hymns;
whom the singers of the Sāman chant with the Vedas, including the auxiliary limbs, the Pada and Krama recitations, and the Upaniṣads.
Salutations to that God whom yogis perceive with minds absorbed in Him through meditation, and whose limit even the hosts of gods and asuras do not know. [Salutations] to Him who,
on His back, was scratched by the sharp edges of the stones of the massive Mount Mandara as it revolved.
May the breath-winds of the Lord, who was sleeping in the form of a tortoise, protect you—
those winds by whose subtle influence the ocean’s waters,
appearing like the shifting tides, continue their tireless coming and going even today without ever resting.
Learn now the origin of the number of Purāṇas, their subject matter and purpose, the gift [of this text], the greatness of that gift, and the merit of reciting it and so forth.
The Brāhma Purāṇa consists of ten thousand verses, and the Pādma Purāṇa consists of fifty-five thousand.
The Śrī-Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa has twenty-three thousand verses, the Śaiva twenty-four;
the Śrī-Bhāgavata has eighteen thousand, the Nārada twenty-five;
the Mārkaṇḍeya nine thousand, and the Vāhnika fifteen thousand four hundred.
The Bhaviṣya Purāṇa shall consist of fourteen thousand and five hundred verses;
the Brahmavaivarta, eighteen thousand; the Laiṅga, eleven thousand;
and the Vārāha, twenty-four thousand and eighty-one thousand verses.
The Skānda Purāṇa is proclaimed to consist of one hundred and one [verses], the Vāmana Purāṇa is said to have ten;
the Kūrma Purāṇa is declared to have seventeen, while the Mātsya Purāṇa has fourteen. The Sauparṇa Purāṇa has nineteen, and the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa has exactly twelve.
Thus, the collection of Purāṇas is said to consist of four hundred thousand verses;
among them, the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam is accepted as comprising eighteen thousand verses.
This was formerly spoken by the Blessed Lord to Brahmā from the lotus of His navel.
Out of compassion, it was revealed to one who remained steadfast yet terrified of worldly existence;
it is joined with narratives of detachment throughout its beginning, middle,
and end, and it delights the virtuous gods with the nectar of the multitude of stories concerning the pastimes of Hari.
That which is the essence of all Vedānta, characterized by the oneness of Brahman and the Self— that non-dual reality— is the foundation of this [work], which has liberation as its sole purpose.
On the full moon day of the month of Bhādrapada, [he gave it] together with a golden lion-throne.
He who gives [a copy of] the Bhāgavata attains the supreme goal.
Other Purāṇas shine among the assembly of the virtuous only so long as the Bhāgavata— the ocean of nectar— is not heard.
Indeed, the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam is held to be the essence of all Vedānta;
for one who is satiated by the nectar of its rasa, there can be no attachment to anything else anywhere.
Just as the Gaṅgā is among rivers, and Acyuta is among the gods;
O twice-born ones, as Śambhu is among the Vaiṣṇavas, and as this [Bhāgavatapurāṇa] is among the Purāṇas; and as Kāśī is indeed unsurpassed among all sacred sites (kṣetra),
so too is the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam among the multitude of Purāṇas.
In this pure Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam Purāṇa, which is dear to the Vaiṣṇavas,
the singular, stainless, and supreme knowledge of the paramahaṃsas is sung; therein,
the state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya), accompanied by knowledge, detachment, and devotion, is revealed.
A person who hears this, recites it well, and is intent on reflecting upon it shall be liberated through devotion.
To whom and by whom was this incomparable lamp of knowledge revealed in the past? It was revealed to the sage Nārada in that form [of Brahmā], and to Kṛṣṇa in His own form.

Out of compassion for the lord of yogis, who has surrendered himself to the Blessed One, let us meditate upon that which is pure, stainless, free from sorrow, immortal, true, and supreme. Salutations to that Blessed One, Vāsudeva, the witness.
Salutations to that Śuka, who is the very embodiment of Brahman, the lord of yogis to whom he [Vyāsa] out of compassion explained this for the sake of one seeking liberation;
he who released Viṣṇurāta, who had been bitten by the serpent of worldly existence.
O Lord of gods, act in such a way that devotion to Your feet may arise in us birth after birth, since You, O Master,
are our protector; for the chanting of Your name is the destroyer of all sins.
Salutation is the pacifier of suffering; I bow down to that supreme Hari.
